rationale: The plasma samples were run in two acquisition batches, and batch shifts in protein intensity can hide the disease signal. This change centres each protein within its batch, using medians from the training fold only, before fitting the same L2 logistic regression. Batch is used only to harmonise features and is never a predictor. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.888.

In DIA plasma data, whether a low-abundance protein is detected at all depends on how much of it there is. Proteins quantified in only 20–70% of samples are currently dropped, so I'm adding their detected/not-detected flags as extra features. The flags are batch-centred like the intensities and down-weighted by 0.5, so this noisier block can't swamp the intensity signal in the same L2 logistic regression.

The median of each sample's observed values depends on how deep that run went: a run that detects more low-abundance proteins gets a lower median, so the median-centring shifts the whole sample. I'll compute the per-sample median only over a fixed reference set of proteins quantified in at least 95% of samples, so the normalization tracks how much material was loaded rather than how many proteins were detected.

I'm giving known AD-related plasma proteins a weaker shrinkage prior in the same L2 logistic regression. After standardisation, their features (intensities and detection flags) are multiplied by 2, which is equivalent to a 4× wider Gaussian prior on their coefficients. With only ~89 samples, this prior on complement, apolipoprotein/lipid-transport, glial/neuronal and acute-phase proteins should help the model find the real signal among about 2,000 noisy features. No new features are added and no label-driven selection is used.

Plasma DIA intensities have heavy-tailed outliers from things like sample handling, hemolysis and platelet contamination, plus fill values in the half-minimum tail. A single extreme sample can pull the L2 logistic regression around when n is about 89. So I'm clipping the standardized intensity features at ±3 SD, a label-free winsorisation fitted on the training fold, before applying the prior weights. That limits each sample's leverage on any one protein and leaves the rest of the pipeline unchanged.

I'm adding four pathway module scores as extra features, each the mean standardised intensity of the measured proteins in one known AD pathway: complement, lipid transport/apolipoproteins, glial/neuronal injury and acute-phase/inflammation. They are weighted like the other prior-biology features (×2). Averaging many correlated proteins should catch coordinated shifts across a pathway with less noise than any single protein. That matters when n is about 89 and individual coefficients are heavily shrunk. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.914.

Plasma MS intensities are often distorted by sample-handling contamination. Red-cell lysis raises haemoglobin, CA1 and PRDX2; platelet activation raises proteins such as TLN1, ITGA2B and MYH9. These shifts move hundreds of proteins at once and have nothing to do with Alzheimer's. This change builds an erythrocyte score and a platelet score for each sample from fixed protein panels. Each protein is regressed on those two scores (fit on the training fold only) and only the residual is kept, before re-standardising and clipping. That should leave a cleaner signal for the same model. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.916.

I'm adding a second, low-dimensional L2 logistic regression that uses only the known-AD-biology features: the prior-pathway proteins and the module scores. Its standardized decision score is averaged with the current full-proteome model. Signal confined to known plasma biology should be estimated more stably at n≈89 than the same proteins competing with ~2,000 noisy features. The full model can still add anything new it finds. Nothing is tuned against the score.

Many low-abundance AD-related plasma proteins, such as GFAP, NEFL, SMOC1, NPTX2, YWHAG and CHI3L1, are quantified in only 20–70% of DIA plasma runs. The prior-biology model never sees them, because it only uses proteins quantified in at least 70% of samples. This change adds the batch-centred detection flags of those mid-detection prior proteins to the prior model, at half weight to match the full model, so whether they are detected (which tracks their abundance) can count in the stably estimated low-dimensional model.

The current module scores take a plain mean of member z-scores, so members that move in opposite directions cancel. In the inflammation module, for example, the positive acute-phase reactants (CRP, HP, SERPINA3, ORM1) fall when the negative ones (TTR, RBP4, AHSG) rise, and the module score then shows little. This change orients each module member by the sign of its loading on the module's first principal component, computed on the training fold without labels, before averaging. Each score then follows the module's dominant coordinated axis instead of a diluted net mean.

The prior-biology model only sees whether mid-detection prior proteins (20–70% quantified, e.g. GFAP, NEFL, SMOC1, CHI3L1 near the detection limit) were detected, not how much was measured. This change adds their intensities to the prior model as left-censored features: missing values get the half-minimum fill, then the values are batch-centred, standardised, clipped and given half weight. Because missingness tracks abundance, this ordering is roughly what a tobit model would use, and it keeps the amount information within detected samples that the binary flag throws away. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.936.

Whether a near-detection-limit protein is detected depends on the protein's own abundance and on how deep each run went, i.e. what fraction of all proteins it quantified. Run depth is a technical, sample-wide factor shared by every detection flag. This change computes each sample's depth (label-free), batch-centres it, and regresses it out of the batch-centred detection flags (OLS fitted on the training fold), so the flags carry protein-specific abundance information rather than a common technical axis.

Right now the two acquisition batches are aligned only in location (per-batch median centring). DIA runs on different batches also tend to differ in dynamic range, so the same biological shift can show up as a bigger or smaller z-score depending on the batch. I'm adding a ComBat-like per-batch scale harmonisation of the intensities, fitted on the training fold only. Each protein's per-batch spread is rescaled to the pooled spread, with that spread estimate first shrunk toward the batch's typical spread across all proteins (an empirical-Bayes style prior worth about 10 samples) and the resulting factor clipped to [0.5, 2]. Batch is still used only to harmonise features, never as a predictor.

I'm adding a nearest-shrunken-centroid (PAM-style diagonal discriminant) scorer as a third ensemble member at weight 0.25. Its soft-threshold delta is chosen by inner grouped CV on the training fold only, and prior-biology features get half the threshold. Both current members are dense L2 logistic models that spread weight across thousands of correlated proteins. A sparse score that ignores correlations and comes from univariate selection is a different kind of model that is known to hold up at n≈70. It should add the few strongly shifted proteins without letting their many weak, noisy neighbours dilute them. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.936.

People's plasma immunoglobulin levels differ a lot (IGHG/IGKC/IGLC constant regions plus their individual-specific V-gene repertoire). That variation moves many protein groups together and isn't specific to AD, much like the erythrocyte and platelet contamination axes whose removal gave +0.0056. This change adds a label-free immunoglobulin-load index as a third nuisance axis and regresses it out with the same training-fold OLS. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.936. One risk: any real Ig–AD signal is also removed from the Ig features.

I'm adding data-driven co-expression module scores to the full-proteome model. Proteins are clustered label-free on the training fold (average-linkage hierarchical clustering on correlation of the cleaned, standardised intensities), and each module of 5 or more proteins becomes one feature, the mean of its members. This follows the WGCNA-style module approach common in AD proteomics. Averaging many co-varying proteins should catch coordinated biology outside the curated pathway list with less noise than single proteins, the same idea that made the curated module scores help in round 6. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.936.

I'm adding a third ensemble member: a low-dimensional L2 logistic regression that uses only the module-level features (the curated pathway scores plus the label-free co-expression module scores). Its standardised decision score is averaged with equal weight alongside the full-proteome and prior-biology models. Module averages pool many correlated proteins, so a model that fits directly on those few dozen scores should estimate coordinated, system-level shifts more stably at n≈89 than when they compete with about 2,000 single-protein features. I haven't run this, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.937.

I'm adding a fifth prior-biology module for the plasma contact-activation, kallikrein–kinin and fibrinogen system (F12, KLKB1, KNG1, F11, HRG, PLG, F2, the SERPINC1/D1/F2 serpins, the C1-inhibitor SERPING1, CPB2 and FGA/FGB/FGG). Published work (Strickland lab) reports that Aβ binds factor XII and fibrinogen, and that contact-system activation, bradykinin release and kininogen cleavage are higher in AD plasma. These proteins are well quantified in plasma MS, so as prior-weighted proteins plus a module score they should give the full model and the prior model a stable, biologically grounded axis. I haven't run it, so I don't know yet whether it beats 0.937.

The two batches may hold different proportions of AD cases. If so, the current per-batch median centring removes part of the real disease difference as if it were a batch effect (the known problem of batch correction under an unbalanced design). I'm changing the batch offsets to be estimated class-balanced on the training fold: in each batch, the per-class medians/means are averaged, as in ComBat with a preserved biological covariate. The test samples get the offsets learned on the training fold, so batch is still used only to harmonise features.

With about 70 training samples per fold and more than 2,000 correlated features, the best L2 strength for the full-proteome model can't be pinned down. Tuning it by inner CV at this n would be very noisy. Instead, I'll average the standardised decision scores of the full model fitted at three regularisation strengths spread geometrically around the current C=0.05 (0.01, 0.05, 0.25). No labels are used to pick C, and this should hedge against a wrong shrinkage level and lower prediction variance. I haven't run this, so I don't know whether it beats 0.937.
